Initiative: Undertake a comprehensive review of emissions and sustainability risk across the supply chain (baseline assessment)
Old Initiative: Undertake a comprehensive review of your emissions in your supply chain and make a plan to reduce them.
Tools: GHG Protocol Scope 3 Calculation Guidance. Helps members establish a Scope 3 emissions baseline, identify relevant value-chain categories and select appropriate calculation methods depending on the data available.
Description: Conduct a baseline assessment of Scope 3 emissions and material sustainability risks across the supply chain, prioritising high-spend, high-emission and high-risk categories. Use the findings to identify data gaps, priority suppliers and reduction opportunities.
Why/Benefit: Establishes a clear Scope 3 baseline, identifies material emissions and sustainability risks, highlights data gaps, and enables resources to be focused on the highest-impact suppliers and categories.
How to achieve this: 1. Map all relevant Scope 3 categories and procurement spend. 2. Calculate an initial footprint using available activity, spend and supplier-specific data. 3. Rank categories and suppliers by emissions, spend and sustainability risk. 4. Identify data gaps and create a prioritised reduction and supplier-engagement plan. 5. Refresh the assessment annually.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of relevant Scope 3 categories assessed, with priority suppliers and reduction opportunities identified
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread applies an inherent risk assessment to 100% of suppliers before conducting more detailed assessment of higher-risk suppliers. Its responsible-sourcing approach demonstrates how a large hospitality operator can systematically screen its supply chain and prioritise higher-risk areas.
Cost Saving/Cost: Primarily staff/consultancy and data-system cost. No universal public cost benchmark; cost depends on supply-chain size, data availability and whether external carbon-accounting support is used.
Carbon Abatement Potential: No direct abatement from assessment alone. It enables subsequent Scope 3 reductions by identifying material hotspots and priority suppliers; abatement should be attributed to actions triggered by the review.
Time to implement/ROI: Initial baseline commonly requires several months depending on data maturity; then refreshed annually. No standalone ROI because this is an enabling/diagnostic action.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % Scope 3 emissions screened; % spend mapped; % supplier-specific data coverage; number/value of priority reduction opportunities identified.

Initiative: Set a Scope 3 emissions reduction target (e.g. aligned to SBTi)
Old Initiative: Set strategic Scope 3 goals, embedded within wider functional team goals, with clear metrics for tracking progress.
Tools: SBTi Supplier Engagement Guidance. Helps members translate Scope 3 ambitions into measurable supplier-related targets, define appropriate coverage and establish a process for tracking progress.
Description: Establish a measurable and time-bound Scope 3 emissions reduction target with a defined baseline year, target year and organisational boundary. Align the target with the Science Based Targets initiative where appropriate.
Why/Benefit: Creates a clear long-term direction for value-chain decarbonisation, supports accountability and investment prioritisation, and provides a credible external benchmark where the target is science-aligned.
How to achieve this: 1. Complete the Scope 3 baseline and identify material categories. 2. Select an absolute reduction, intensity or supplier-engagement target consistent with recognised guidance. 3. Define baseline year, target year, boundary and calculation method. 4. Obtain executive approval and, where appropriate, submit to SBTi. 5. Track and disclose progress annually.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Scope 3 target coverage as % of total Scope 3 emissions, with target-year progress tracked annually
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi requires companies whose Scope 3 emissions exceed the relevant threshold to set Scope 3 targets; supplier-engagement and/or reduction targets should collectively cover at least 67% of total Scope 3 emissions under current criteria.
Cost Saving/Cost: Internal target-setting cost is generally low, but inventory improvement, SBTi validation and implementation require staff and potentially consultancy/data costs. No universal ROI.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially high over the target period, but the target itself does not reduce emissions. Actual abatement depends on the portfolio of procurement, supplier and product interventions used to deliver it.
Time to implement/ROI: Target design can be completed over several months once a credible baseline exists. ROI is realised through the underlying reduction initiatives, not the target-setting exercise itself.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % Scope 3 covered by target; annual % reduction vs baseline; tCO2e reduced; % target trajectory achieved.

Initiative: Establish a sustainable procurement policy, approved and sponsored at Board/ExCo level
Tools: ISO 20400 Sustainable Procurement Guidance. Helps members integrate sustainability principles into procurement policies, governance, decision-making and purchasing processes.
Description: Develop and approve a sustainable procurement policy that defines environmental and social requirements, governance responsibilities and decision-making criteria for purchasing goods and services. Ensure the policy is supported by an appropriate senior governance body.
Why/Benefit: Provides a consistent governance framework for procurement decisions, embeds sustainability into purchasing standards, strengthens accountability and reduces environmental, social and reputational supply-chain risks.
How to achieve this: 1. Define policy scope, principles and priority environmental/social requirements. 2. Assign procurement and sustainability responsibilities. 3. Consult category teams, legal and key stakeholders. 4. Obtain Board/ExCo or equivalent senior approval. 5. Integrate the policy into sourcing, tenders, contracts and supplier reviews. 6. Review periodically.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Sustainable procurement policy approved, communicated and applied to % of addressable procurement spend
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread operates a responsible-sourcing framework with commodity-specific sourcing policies and supplier due diligence. Its responsible-sourcing page states that 100% of suppliers undergo inherent risk assessment, illustrating policy application across a large hospitality supply base.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low direct capex; primarily policy development, legal/procurement staff time and implementation costs. No standalone carbon-payback figure is publicly disclosed.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect. The policy enables emissions and risk reductions through sourcing requirements, but carbon savings should be attributed to the specific procurement changes it drives.
Time to implement/ROI: Policy development and approval can typically be completed within months; full application across procurement may take one or more contract cycles. No universal ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % addressable spend covered; % tenders/contracts applying policy; supplier compliance rate; number of policy exceptions.

Initiative: Implement a regular cadence of touchpoints between procurement, sustainability, and category teams to drive Responsible Procurement priorities
Tools: Internal governance process. No specific external tool is required. Members can implement this through regular cross-functional meetings, clear ownership, action tracking and performance reviews.
Description: Establish regular cross-functional meetings between procurement, sustainability and category teams to review responsible procurement priorities, supplier performance, risks, actions and delivery responsibilities.
Why/Benefit: Improves coordination and accountability, helps sustainability information influence commercial decisions, and reduces the risk that supplier actions stall between functions.
How to achieve this: 1. Establish monthly or quarterly governance meetings. 2. Maintain a shared dashboard covering priority suppliers, data gaps, risks and actions. 3. Assign action owners and deadlines. 4. Escalate material issues to senior governance. 5. Review progress and update priorities at each meeting.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of planned cross-functional responsible procurement meetings held, with actions closed by due date
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi supplier-engagement guidance highlights the need for internal alignment, clear ownership and structured programmes before and during supplier engagement. This provides an evidence base for regular cross-functional governance even where companies do not disclose meeting cadence publicly.
Cost Saving/Cost: Very low direct cost; mainly staff time and dashboard/reporting effort.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect/enabling. No defensible generic tCO2e saving can be assigned to meetings themselves; impact comes from faster delivery of procurement and supplier actions.
Time to implement/ROI: Can be established within weeks. No formal ROI; operational benefit should be measured through action closure and delivery performance.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % meetings held; % actions closed on time; number of escalated issues resolved; tCO2e/value delivered by actions governed through the forum.

Initiative: Build sustainable procurement training and capability into the wider procurement team's professional development
Old Initiative: Hire specialist sustainability resource inside your procurement team.
Tools: CDP Supplier Engagement Guidance. Provides practical guidance on supplier engagement, data collection and climate-related supply-chain management that can support procurement-team capability building and training.
Description: Provide role-specific sustainable procurement training for procurement and category teams, covering Scope 3 emissions, supplier engagement, environmental risks, responsible sourcing standards and the use of sustainability criteria in purchasing decisions.
Why/Benefit: Builds internal capability so sustainability criteria are consistently applied in sourcing decisions, reduces dependence on a small specialist team and improves the quality of supplier engagement and data requests.
How to achieve this: 1. Assess capability gaps by procurement role. 2. Develop role-specific modules on Scope 3, sourcing standards, supplier data and category risks. 3. Integrate training into onboarding and professional development. 4. Provide practical category tools and templates. 5. Track completion and assess application through procurement reviews.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of relevant procurement and category staff completing role-specific sustainable procurement training
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi cites AstraZeneca's supplier programme, which uses webinars, training, supplier resources and clear reporting expectations; the programme was associated with an 18% increase in suppliers reporting emissions to CDP.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low to moderate cost depending on whether training is developed internally or externally. Costs are mainly staff time, training design and delivery.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect. Training does not itself create a reliable carbon saving; abatement comes from improved sourcing and supplier decisions made by trained teams.
Time to implement/ROI: Initial training can be designed and rolled out within months, then repeated annually/onboarding. No standalone ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % staff trained; assessment/pass rate; % sourcing events applying sustainability criteria; supplier-data response/quality improvement.

Old Initiative: Introduce a supplier engagement platform, with a system for monitoring, accountability and support for suppliers.
Tools: CDP Supply Chain. Helps members collect standardised climate and sustainability information from suppliers, identify data gaps and improve visibility of supplier performance.
Description: Establish a standardised process for collecting relevant emissions and sustainability data from priority suppliers through questionnaires, reporting platforms, contractual requirements or direct engagement. Define minimum data requirements and monitor supplier response and data quality.
Why/Benefit: Improves Scope 3 accuracy, reduces reliance on spend-based estimates, identifies supplier-specific hotspots and creates the information needed to track supplier progress and target engagement.
How to achieve this: 1. Define priority supplier population and minimum data fields. 2. Select collection route such as questionnaire, CDP/platform or direct template. 3. Communicate requirements and deadlines. 4. Provide guidance and support. 5. Validate completeness and quality. 6. Integrate accepted data into the Scope 3 inventory and supplier scorecards.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority suppliers providing requested sustainability data, with % meeting minimum data-quality requirements
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi reports that AstraZeneca's structured supplier engagement—including reporting expectations, training and support—produced an 18% increase in suppliers reporting emissions to CDP.
Cost Saving/Cost: Variable. Internal questionnaires can be low cost; specialist supplier-data platforms and assurance add subscription, onboarding and staff costs. No universal public benchmark.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect initially, but essential for identifying and verifying supplier reductions. No generic abatement factor should be assigned to data collection itself.
Time to implement/ROI: Basic collection can begin within months; achieving high-quality supplier-specific coverage is usually multi-year. ROI comes from better decisions, compliance and verified reductions rather than direct savings.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % priority suppliers responding; % supplier spend/emissions covered by primary data; % data meeting quality threshold; reduction in estimated-data share.

Initiative: Conduct lifecycle assessments (LCA) and collect product carbon footprints on key commodities to understand emissions at ingredient level
Old Initiative: Conduct LCAs on specific commodities to understand your emissions at ingredient level.
Tools: GHG Protocol Product Life Cycle Accounting and Reporting Standard. Provides a consistent methodology for quantifying product-level emissions and helps members compare carbon impacts across commodities or products using defined system boundaries.
Description: Collect product carbon footprint data or conduct lifecycle assessments for priority high-emission commodities and products. Use the results to identify emissions hotspots, compare sourcing options and support lower-impact procurement decisions.
Why/Benefit: Provides product-level evidence for comparing suppliers and ingredients, improves the accuracy of Scope 3 calculations and enables targeted recipe, sourcing and supplier interventions.
How to achieve this: 1. Prioritise commodities by emissions/spend. 2. Define consistent functional units and lifecycle boundaries. 3. Request supplier PCFs/EPDs or commission LCAs where needed. 4. Review methodology and data quality. 5. Compare hotspots and alternatives. 6. Integrate results into sourcing and product decisions.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority commodities covered by product carbon footprints or LCAs meeting defined quality criteria
Evidence/Case Study: The GHG Protocol Scope 3 framework supports progressively improving purchased-goods data from secondary estimates toward supplier/product-specific information. SBTi supplier guidance similarly stresses better supplier emissions data as a foundation for value-chain action.
Cost Saving/Cost: Moderate to high analytical cost where bespoke LCAs are commissioned; lower where credible supplier PCFs already exist. Cost varies by product complexity, number of SKUs and assurance level.
Carbon Abatement Potential: No direct abatement from measurement. High decision-support potential because LCAs can identify lower-carbon ingredients/suppliers; savings must be calculated from the sourcing or product change selected.
Time to implement/ROI: Individual studies can take weeks to months; portfolio coverage is usually phased. ROI depends on whether results lead to lower-cost/lower-carbon sourcing or product reformulation.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % priority commodities with quality-assured PCFs/LCA; % spend/emissions covered; kgCO2e/kg or serving; number of sourcing changes informed by LCA.

Initiative: Set supplier-facing requirements (Supplier codes of conduct) and communicate shared targets
Old Initiative: Build carbon reduction and sustainability challenges into supplier contracts.; Communicate your Scope 3 goals to suppliers and set them goals.
Tools: SBTi Supplier Engagement Guidance. Helps members structure climate expectations for suppliers, communicate emissions targets and develop an approach for supplier target-setting and engagement.
Description: Incorporate sustainability requirements into supplier codes of conduct, contracts, tender documents, onboarding processes and performance expectations. Communicate relevant Scope 3 targets and clarify the actions and data expected from suppliers.
Why/Benefit: Creates clear and consistent supplier expectations, strengthens accountability, embeds sustainability into commercial relationships and helps align suppliers with the organisation's Scope 3 pathway.
How to achieve this: 1. Define minimum supplier sustainability requirements. 2. Embed them in the supplier code, tenders and contracts. 3. Communicate Scope 3 targets and reporting expectations. 4. Provide implementation guidance. 5. Monitor acceptance/compliance and escalate gaps. 6. Update requirements as standards mature.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of addressable supplier spend covered by an approved supplier code, contractual sustainability clauses or communicated targets
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi cites AstraZeneca's clear supplier standards and reporting expectations. Its programme contributed to an 18% increase in suppliers reporting emissions to CDP, illustrating the effect of clear requirements combined with support.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low to moderate implementation cost, mainly legal/procurement time, supplier communication and monitoring. Commercial impacts depend on supplier response and contract design.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect but potentially high across material suppliers. Requirements create the mechanism for reductions, but verified abatement must be measured from supplier actions.
Time to implement/ROI: Can be introduced in new tenders immediately and rolled through existing contracts over renewal cycles; full coverage may take several years. No generic ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % spend under requirements; % suppliers acknowledging code/targets; % suppliers reporting emissions; % suppliers with reduction targets; tCO2e reduced.

Initiative: Use a supplier scorecard to track performance and prioritise engagement with material suppliers
Old Initiative: Introduce a supplier engagement platform, with a system for monitoring, accountability and support for suppliers.
Tools: EcoVadis Sustainability Ratings. Provides supplier sustainability scorecards that can help members assess performance, compare suppliers and prioritise engagement with material or higher-risk suppliers.
Description: Introduce a supplier sustainability scorecard covering relevant indicators such as emissions data, target-setting, compliance, certifications, risk and improvement progress. Use the results to monitor performance and prioritise engagement with material suppliers.
Why/Benefit: Creates a comparable view of supplier performance, focuses limited engagement resources on the most material gaps and enables sustainability performance to influence supplier reviews and sourcing decisions.
How to achieve this: 1. Select a concise set of material scorecard indicators. 2. Weight metrics by category/risk where appropriate. 3. Populate using supplier data and evidence. 4. Review scores with suppliers at least annually. 5. Agree corrective/improvement actions. 6. Link results to sourcing and preferred-supplier decisions where appropriate.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority suppliers assessed through the scorecard and % with agreed improvement actions
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi supplier-engagement guidance recommends segmenting suppliers, setting clear expectations, tracking progress and adapting engagement based on supplier performance. This supports a scorecard approach even where a hospitality-specific quantified case is not publicly disclosed.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low to moderate if built into existing procurement systems; higher if a third-party ratings/platform service is purchased. No universal public cost.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect. Scorecards enable prioritisation and accountability; carbon impact comes from the improvement actions suppliers implement.
Time to implement/ROI: Can be designed and piloted within months; mature scorecard programmes develop over annual supplier-review cycles. No standalone ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % priority suppliers scored; average/median score; % with improvement plans; % actions completed; % spend with high-performing suppliers.

Initiative: Provide a tailored supplier engagement strategy for material/priority suppliers (segmented by spend, risk, and emissions contribution)
Old Initiative: Map your key suppliers with key commodities and identify which suppliers need help.; Work with suppliers to understand your emissions and identify opportunities for emissions reductions.
Tools: SBTi Supplier Engagement Guidance and CDP Supplier Engagement Guidance. Help members identify priority suppliers and develop differentiated engagement approaches based on emissions, spend, strategic importance and supplier capability.
Description: Segment suppliers according to procurement spend, emissions contribution, sustainability risk and strategic importance. Develop differentiated engagement plans for priority supplier groups, including data requests, meetings, training, improvement plans and commercial incentives.
Why/Benefit: Directs engagement effort toward suppliers that matter most, improves supplier support and increases the likelihood that limited procurement and sustainability resources deliver measurable Scope 3 progress.
How to achieve this: 1. Segment suppliers by spend, emissions, risk and strategic importance. 2. Define engagement tiers. 3. Set tailored asks for each tier, from basic data disclosure to science-based targets and joint projects. 4. Provide support and training. 5. Track progress and re-segment annually.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority supplier groups with a documented engagement plan and % of planned actions completed
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi supplier-engagement guidance provides a structured approach to evaluating suppliers, developing targets and implementing differentiated engagement programmes. AstraZeneca's supplier programme demonstrates the use of targeted resources and reporting expectations.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low to moderate programme cost; primarily staff time, supplier workshops, data tools and support. Cost rises with the depth of one-to-one engagement.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially high where engagement is concentrated on suppliers responsible for a large share of Scope 3 emissions. Actual abatement must be measured from supplier reductions.
Time to implement/ROI: Segmentation can be completed in months; supplier improvement is typically multi-year. ROI depends on emissions reductions, resilience and commercial benefits achieved.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % priority suppliers with engagement plans; % actions completed; % supplier emissions covered; % suppliers setting targets; tCO2e reduced.

Initiative: Incentivise supplier progress (e.g. preferred status, longer contracts)
Old Initiative: Incentivise suppliers to encourage emission reductions.
Tools: SBTi Supplier Engagement Guidance and Case Studies. Provides examples of how businesses can combine supplier requirements, support and incentives to encourage progress against climate targets.
Description: Link supplier sustainability performance and improvement to commercial or non-commercial incentives, such as preferred supplier status, longer contracts, increased procurement opportunities, recognition or access to support programmes.
Why/Benefit: Strengthens the commercial case for supplier action, rewards verified progress and helps move sustainability from a reporting request into a meaningful part of the supplier relationship.
How to achieve this: 1. Define performance thresholds eligible for incentives. 2. Select incentives proportionate to supplier/category importance. 3. Communicate rules transparently. 4. Verify performance before rewards are granted. 5. Review whether incentives change supplier behaviour and refine the scheme.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority suppliers eligible for incentives and % showing verified improvement after incentives are introduced
Evidence/Case Study: SBTi supplier-engagement guidance recommends using procurement levers and structured engagement to motivate suppliers. Public hospitality-specific quantified results for preferred-status incentives are limited, so this is best treated as a guidance-backed mechanism rather than a quantified peer case.
Cost Saving/Cost: Variable. Non-financial recognition can be low cost; longer contracts or increased volumes create commercial commitments and opportunity costs rather than simple programme fees.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially material if incentives drive supplier target-setting and operational reductions, but no generic tCO2e factor is defensible.
Time to implement/ROI: Can be incorporated into supplier reviews/tenders within months; measurable supplier performance change may require 1–3+ years. ROI is supplier/category-specific.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % eligible suppliers improving; % spend with incentivised high performers; supplier target/data coverage; verified tCO2e reductions following incentives.

Initiative: Co-invest with suppliers in decarbonisation or regenerative agriculture projects (e.g. insetting programmes)
Old Initiative: Support on-farm GHG mitigation and sustainable farming techniques such as regenerative agriculture in your supply chain.
Tools: Value Change Initiative (VCI) Guidance. Helps members design and account for value-chain interventions, including supplier decarbonisation and insetting projects, and link interventions to Scope 3 emissions outcomes.
Description: Collaborate with strategic suppliers to finance or support projects that reduce supply-chain emissions or improve agricultural practices. Examples may include energy-efficiency projects, renewable energy, regenerative agriculture, low-carbon inputs or credible insetting programmes.
Why/Benefit: Can unlock reductions that suppliers may not be able to finance alone, strengthens strategic supplier relationships and can generate measurable value-chain emissions reductions or removals.
How to achieve this: 1. Identify high-emission suppliers/commodities and feasible projects. 2. Agree funding, ownership, baselines and measurement methodology. 3. Define how carbon benefits are allocated and claimed. 4. Implement with suppliers/farmers and technical partners. 5. Monitor verified outcomes and scale successful projects.
KPI (Measurable Objective): Annual investment in supplier decarbonisation projects and verified tCO2e reduced or removed within the value chain
Evidence/Case Study: McDonald's and partners supported a five-year Nebraska regenerative-agriculture programme with a joint investment of US$8.5 million, targeting 100,000 acres and an estimated sequestration potential of 75,000 metric tonnes of carbon.
Cost Saving/Cost: Potentially significant investment. Peer example: US$8.5m joint project funding. Costs vary greatly by commodity, geography, intervention and co-funding structure.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially high. McDonald's case cited an estimated 75,000 metric tonnes of carbon sequestration potential, but this is projected potential rather than verified achieved reduction.
Time to implement/ROI: Typically multi-year; McDonald's example is a five-year programme. Financial ROI may be indirect through resilience/productivity, while carbon ROI should be tracked as cost per verified tCO2e.
Efficiency/Impact measure: £/$ invested; acres/hectares covered; suppliers/farms participating; verified tCO2e reduced/removed; £ per tCO2e; yield/resilience indicators.

Initiative: Map supply chains beyond Tier 1 (Tier 2/3, down to farm/origin level) for material (High-spend, high-carbon and/or high-risk commodities)
Old Initiative: Map your key suppliers with key commodities and identify which suppliers need help.
Tools: Trase. Helps members investigate commodity supply chains, sourcing regions and upstream environmental exposure, supporting supply-chain mapping beyond immediate Tier 1 suppliers.
Description: Trace priority high-spend, high-emission or high-risk commodities beyond direct suppliers to Tier 2, Tier 3 and, where feasible, farm or origin level. Use the mapping to identify environmental risks, traceability gaps and opportunities for targeted intervention.
Why/Benefit: Improves visibility of risks and emissions hidden beyond direct suppliers, supports due diligence and enables interventions to be directed at the actual producers or processors responsible for impacts.
How to achieve this: 1. Prioritise commodities using spend, carbon and sustainability risk. 2. Request upstream supplier and origin information from Tier 1 suppliers. 3. Map processors, traders and producers. 4. Validate traceability evidence. 5. Flag gaps/high-risk origins and develop remediation plans. 6. Refresh mapping periodically.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of material high-risk commodities traceable to Tier 2/3 or origin, with identified high-risk gaps under action
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread uses commodity-specific sourcing requirements and supply-chain due diligence, including farm-assurance requirements for primary proteins and commitments linked to deforestation-risk commodities, demonstrating the importance of traceability beyond direct purchasing relationships.
Cost Saving/Cost: Moderate to high depending on supply-chain complexity, supplier cooperation, traceability platforms and assurance needs. No universal cost benchmark.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect. Mapping itself does not reduce emissions but enables targeted sourcing, deforestation and supplier interventions. Carbon impact should be assigned to those subsequent actions.
Time to implement/ROI: Simple commodity maps can be developed in months; deep farm/origin traceability can take multiple years. No standalone ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % volume/spend traceable to Tier 2/3/origin; number of high-risk gaps; % gaps under remediation; % supplier data verified.

Initiative: Map exposure to forest-risk commodities (soy, palm oil, cocoa, coffee, beef/leather, rubber, timber/paper & packaging)
Tools: Global Forest Watch Pro and Trase. Help members identify sourcing locations and screen commodity supply chains for deforestation and forest-related environmental risks.
Description: Identify where forest-risk commodities such as soy, palm oil, cocoa, coffee, beef, leather, rubber, timber, paper and packaging occur within the supply chain. Assess procurement volumes, sourcing locations, suppliers, traceability and potential deforestation or conversion risks.
Why/Benefit: Identifies where deforestation risk is concentrated, supports compliance and due diligence, and provides the baseline needed to prioritise traceability, certification and supplier action.
How to achieve this: 1. Build a commodity inventory across direct and embedded ingredients/materials. 2. Quantify spend/volume and suppliers. 3. Identify sourcing countries/regions. 4. Screen geographic and commodity deforestation risk. 5. Prioritise high-risk combinations for traceability and supplier action. 6. Update annually.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of relevant procurement spend or volume screened for forest-risk commodities and sourcing-location risk
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread publishes commodity-specific responsible-sourcing requirements covering palm oil, coffee, meat, fish and other priority products and has an SBTi no-deforestation commitment for its primary deforestation-linked commodity.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low to moderate for an initial desk-based screen; higher where specialist traceability datasets, geospatial tools or assurance are needed.
Carbon Abatement Potential: No direct abatement from risk mapping. It enables deforestation-free sourcing and supplier interventions, which can have significant land-use emissions benefits.
Time to implement/ROI: Initial screening can be completed within months; detailed origin-level mapping may take longer. No standalone ROI.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % forest-risk spend/volume screened; % with known origin; number/value of high-risk commodity-country combinations; % high-risk exposure under action.

Initiative: Set a deforestation-free sourcing commitment and require traceability to origin
Old Initiative: Commit to zero deforestation in your supply chain.; Adopt strategies to promote deforestation free value chain.
Tools: Accountability Framework initiative (AFi). Provides practical guidance for setting credible deforestation- and conversion-free commitments, establishing traceability requirements and monitoring implementation across supply chains.
Description: Establish a time-bound commitment to source priority commodities without deforestation or ecosystem conversion. Define the commodities and supply-chain scope covered, require traceability to origin and set expectations for supplier compliance and verification.
Why/Benefit: Creates a clear standard for high-risk commodities, reduces exposure to land-use and reputational risk, supports regulatory readiness and drives improved traceability and supplier practices.
How to achieve this: 1. Define covered commodities, geographies and cut-off dates. 2. Establish traceability and verification requirements. 3. Incorporate requirements into supplier contracts/policies. 4. Collect origin data and assess compliance. 5. Remediate non-compliance and disclose progress annually.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of priority forest-risk commodity volume covered by the commitment and traceable to origin or an accepted control point
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread states a commitment to no deforestation across its primary deforestation-linked commodity with a target date of 31 December 2025. It also publishes commodity-specific sourcing requirements, including RSPO palm oil and certified coffee.
Cost Saving/Cost: Low direct policy cost but potentially material sourcing, traceability and assurance costs. Price effects vary by commodity and supplier.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Potentially high for land-use intensive commodities, but no generic tCO2e saving should be assigned without commodity, origin and counterfactual data.
Time to implement/ROI: Policy can be established within months; achieving verified origin-level compliance across complex commodities can take several years. ROI is mainly risk/resilience and avoided land-use impact rather than a standard payback.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % commodity volume covered; % traceable to origin/control point; % verified deforestation-free; number of non-compliance cases remediated.

Initiative: Source certified sustainable commodities (e.g. RSPO for palm oil, Rainforest Alliance/UTZ or 4C for coffee and cocoa, FSC/PEFC for timber and paper-based packaging)
Old Initiative: Introduce certification to demonstrate responsible sourcing and deforestation avoidance
Tools: RSPO, Rainforest Alliance, FSC and PEFC certification and Chain of Custody resources. Help members select appropriate certification schemes for different commodities and verify that certified products are traceable through the supply chain.
Description: Increase sourcing of priority commodities through recognised certification schemes or other credible verification mechanisms. Use certification alongside traceability, supplier due diligence and sourcing requirements rather than as a substitute for a broader responsible sourcing strategy.
Why/Benefit: Provides recognised third-party assurance, improves traceability and minimum sourcing standards, supports customer and stakeholder confidence, and can reduce exposure to environmental and social risks in high-risk commodities.
How to achieve this: 1. Identify priority commodities and approved schemes. 2. Establish baseline certified volume/spend. 3. Add certification requirements to specifications and contracts. 4. Verify chain-of-custody documentation. 5. Track certified volume and close gaps. 6. Combine certification with origin traceability and due diligence.
KPI (Measurable Objective): % of relevant commodity volume certified or otherwise verified against an approved sustainability standard
Evidence/Case Study: Whitbread reports that 100% of wild-caught fish served is MSC certified, 100% of UK coffee is Fairtrade or Rainforest Alliance certified, and it has targeted 100% RSPO-certified palm oil in own-recipe products by the end of 2025.
Cost Saving/Cost: Certification may involve supplier premiums, audit/chain-of-custody fees and administration. Costs vary by scheme and commodity; no single benchmark is appropriate.
Carbon Abatement Potential: Certification is not a generic carbon-abatement factor. Carbon and land-use benefits depend on the standard, commodity, origin and actual production improvements achieved.
Time to implement/ROI: Can be phased through procurement and contract cycles over months to several years. No universal ROI; value includes assurance, risk reduction and market/customer benefits.
Efficiency/Impact measure: % commodity volume/spend certified; % chain-of-custody verified; number of priority commodities covered; % certified volume with origin traceability.
